title: Concept Drills — Microbes in Human Welfare (Class 12 Biology)
subject: biology

questions.question: Why do yeast cells convert sugar to ethanol rather than fully oxidising it to CO₂ and water, and what does the brewer gain from this?
questions.solution: Yeast ferments anaerobically (or when sugar is abundant) because it regenerates NAD⁺ without oxygen — ethanol and CO₂ are the by-products of that redox balancing. The brewer harvests the ethanol as the product and the CO₂ for carbonation. Incomplete oxidation is the price of energy without oxygen, and it is exactly what industry wants.

questions.question: Why does milk curdle with Lactobacillus, and why does the curd keep longer than fresh milk?
questions.solution: Lactobacillus converts lactose to lactic acid; the falling pH makes casein micelles coagulate into curd. The acid also inhibits spoilage and pathogenic bacteria — a natural preservative mechanism. Souring is a controlled microbial shift, which is why curd is both a food and a mild probiotic.

questions.question: Penicillin kills bacteria but not the patient. What structural difference does it exploit, and why is the same trick harder against fungi or viruses?
questions.solution: Penicillin blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking in the bacterial CELL WALL — a structure human cells lack (we have membranes, no wall). That asymmetry is selective toxicity. Fungi are eukaryotes sharing most human biochemistry (fewer unique targets); viruses use HOST machinery entirely, so inhibiting 'the virus' usually means inhibiting yourself. Unique microbial structures are the only safe drug targets.

questions.question: Why must a biogas plant exclude oxygen, and what does the methanogen stage contribute that the acid-forming stage does not?
questions.solution: The whole consortium is anaerobic: aerobic microbes would simply oxidise the organic matter to CO₂, wasting the energy. Acid-forming bacteria hydrolyse and ferment complex waste into organic acids; METHANOGENS (strict anaerobes, e.g. Methanobacterium) then convert those acids/CO₂ into CH₄ — the fuel. Two specialised stages under oxygen exclusion yield a burnable gas instead of heat.

questions.question: Rhizobium in legume nodules and Anabaena in ferns both 'fix nitrogen'. Compare the two partnerships and what each contributes to the field.
questions.solution: Rhizobium lives symbiotically in legume ROOT NODULES, exchanging fixed nitrogen for plant photosynthate — enriching soil when the crop residues decompose. Anabaena (with its heterocysts) associates with the water fern Azolla in PADDIES, fixing N in flooded conditions where legumes cannot grow. Two different crops, two different niches — both replace fertiliser N biologically.

questions.question: Why is Baculovirus (NPV) considered a safer pest control than chemical insecticide? Focus on host range.
questions.solution: Baculoviruses of the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus infect only insects — often a SINGLE species or narrow group — so they remove the pest without killing pollinators, predators or beneficial insects. Broad-spectrum chemicals kill everything, triggering pest resurgence and residue problems. Narrow host range is the safety property; integrated pest management exploits it.

questions.question: Why does sewage treatment need BOTH primary physical settling AND secondary biological treatment? What does each remove?
questions.solution: Primary treatment is PHYSICAL: screens and grit/settling tanks remove floating and settleable solids — the bulk mass, but dissolved organic matter stays. Secondary treatment is BIOLOGICAL: aeration tanks let aerobic microbes (flocs) oxidise the dissolved organics into biomass (activated sludge), dropping the BOD. Physical removal cannot touch dissolved pollution; biology handles what physics leaves behind.

questions.concept: Industrial products — which microbe makes what
questions.question: Match four industrial microbial products to their producers: citric acid, ethanol, streptomycin, statins — and say what the microbe's role is in each.
questions.solution: Citric acid — Aspergillus niger (a mould); ethanol — Saccharomyces (yeast) fermenting sugars; streptomycin — Streptomyces (an actinomycete bacterium); statins — Monascus/yeast (competitive inhibitor of HMG-CoA reductase, lowering cholesterol). In each case the microbe's own metabolism is harvested: its acid, alcohol, antibiotic or secondary metabolite becomes the product.
